newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS-Danish budget wrangling worries markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Danish budget wrangling worries markets.

text.p: With only four weeks left on the parliamentary calendar, Denmark's minority government is still trying to nurse its 1997 budget through the assembly and the process is making securities markets uneasy.
The centre-left coalition was forced to seek piecemeal backing for individual budget elements after it failed to win support for a comprehensive package from the opposition conservatives.

Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft has said that he plans to bring the public sector deficit into balance in 1997, from its 1996 deficit of 5.8 billion Danish crowns ($1 billion). The talks with the Conservatives foundered on where to make specific savings.

The first of the budget's stripped-down components, a 0.1 increase in gross income tax to 8.0 percent, became law on Thursday by 62 votes to 52, passing only with support from the far-left Socialist People's Party and Unity List.

It is the government's growing dependence on the anti-capitalist left which seems to worry the markets more than the slow pace of legislation, which must be completed by the December 19 Christmas recess.

"With leftist parties getting involved in the budget negotiations there is not really any way that (Danish bonds) can pull their weight and there's no chance of narrowing the yield gap to Germany", a bond dealer said on Thursday.
The benchmark 10-year government eight percent bond closed down 0.09 point on Thursday and the six percent mortgage bond due in 2026 slumped 0.35 point to 84.80.

The stock market has also attributed recent falls to budget anxiety, both because of the overall political uncertainty and also due to specific proposals such as one, shelved for now, to tax yields on shares held in a pension scheme.

The price of the left's support for Thursday's gross tax rise, estimated to put an extra 610 million in treasury coffers next year, is a government promise to pay local authorities 25,000 crowns every time they transfer an employee from state-maintained work schemes to a "real" job.
The money is to be paid from the support budget for local authorities.

Next on the government agenda is an offer to meet Liberal and Conservative demands for a 400 million crown increase in hospital budgets in return for their pledges of overall budget support in parliament.

There is so far no proposal on how to finance the increase, although an agreement by the pharmaceutical industry to lower medicine prices is expected to bring the government savings of 100 million in reduced subsidies of prescription medicine.
After preliminary talks on Wednesday the two opposition parties said that a deal on hospital budgets was possible without any pledge to support the government on the rest of the budget.
The right and centre-right parties, known to Danes as the bourgeois opposition, hold a total of 83 seats in the 179-seat parliament, to the ruling coalition's 76.

The leftist fringe, holding the balance of power with a total of 19 seats, became feisty in a recent row over the government's bungled attempt to block a visit by British author Salman Rushdie and seriously considered voting with the right in a vote of no confidence.
Most analysts, however, doubt that the left would risk forcing a general election which could well return a right-wing government.
